translations.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over Persia in the great city of Nineveh, in the days of Arphaxad, who ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana.

He built a wall around Ecbatana with hewn stones. Its foundation was thirty cubits wide toward the outside of the city and sixty cubits wide toward the city. He made the wall seventy cubits high and its corners fifty cubits.
He erected towers by the gate, each a hundred cubits high, with foundations sixty cubits from corner to corner.
He made the openings of its gates seventy cubits high and thirty cubits wide, so that his mighty men, his strong warriors, and his infantry forces could enter.
In those days Nebuchadnezzar fought against Arphaxad, the great king, in the great plain situated in the territory of Ragau.

All who lived in the mountains joined him, together with all those in the mountains of the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hydaspes, and in the fields of Arioch, king of Elymais. Very many nations gathered to fight against the Chaldeans.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia, sent to all who lived in the territory of Persia and to all who lived to their west: those living in Cilicia, Damascus, and Lebanon, and all those living toward the coast.
He also sent to the nations living in Carmel and Gilead, in Upper Galilee, and in the great plain of Esdraelon;
to all who lived in Samaria and its towns, and those beyond the Jordan as far as Jerusalem, Betane, Chelous, Kadesh, the river of Egypt, Tahpanhes, Rameses, and the whole land of Goshen;
as far as the region above Tanis and Memphis, and to all those in Egypt as far as the border of Ethiopia.

All who lived throughout the land rejected the command of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia, and did not go with him to war, because they did not fear him. In their eyes he was like an ordinary man, and his messengers returned from their presence naked and disgraced.

Nebuchadnezzar became very angry with that entire land. He swore by his royal throne that he would take vengeance on all the territory of Cilicia, Damascus, and Syria, killing them with the sword, and on all who lived in the land of Moab, the Ammonites, all Judah, and everyone in Egypt, as far as the borders of the two lands.
In the seventeenth year he fought against King Arphaxad with his army, defeated him, and brought in all his forces, all his horses, and all his chariots.
He mustered his cities and marched as far as Ecbatana. He captured their towers until he had ravaged the city and taken it.
He captured Arphaxad in the region of Rages, pierced him with a spear, and destroyed him forever.
He and all those with him entered, a great multitude of fighting men. He remained there for a hundred and twenty days, deliberating and making plans.

In the eighteenth year, on the seventh day of the waning moon in the first month, a decision was made in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia, to take vengeance on the whole earth, just as he had said.
He summoned all his officials and envoys, discussed his secret plan with them, and spoke of all the harm he would bring upon the earth.
They resolved to destroy all flesh among those who had not complied with the word of his mouth.
After this, when he had finished his deliberations, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia, summoned Holofernes, the commander of his army, who served under him.

He said to him: This is what the great king, lord of every land, says: You shall now leave my presence and take with you men confident in their strength: a hundred and two thousand infantrymen, a hundred and two thousand horsemen with their horses, and a hundred and two thousand archers.
You shall go out from me into all the land to the west, because they refused to obey the word of my mouth.

Proclaim to them that they must prepare earth and water for me, because I am coming against them in my wrath. I will cover the face of the earth with the feet of my army and make them spoil and plunder.
Their corpses will fill their valleys; their corpses will fill the rivers and the great river as well.
I will scatter their captives to the ends of the earth.
But you shall go ahead and seize all their territory for me. They shall surrender themselves to you, and you shall keep them for me until the day when I take vengeance on them.
Let your eye show no pity to those who resist. Kill them and plunder them throughout your land.
As surely as I live and my kingdom stands firm, I will do this with my own hands, just as I have said.
You must not leave out even one word of your lord's command. Carry out what I have commanded you, and do not delay in doing it.
Holofernes left his lord's presence and summoned all the mighty men, all the officers and soldiers, and the commanders of his army and of Assyria.
He counted the chosen fighting men, as his master had commanded: 102,000 infantry and 102,000 archers.
He commanded them all to fight and wage war.
They took very many camels, donkeys, and mules to carry their provisions, and countless sheep, cattle, and goats for their food.
He supplied all his men, and many others, with very large amounts of gold and silver from the king’s house.
He went out with his entire army and marched to war from the presence of King Nebuchadnezzar, to cover the whole face of the earth toward the west with chariots, horses, and chosen infantry.
The many people who joined them went out with them like locusts and like the sand of the sea. They were so numerous that they could not be counted.
They went out from Nineveh on a three-day journey into the wilderness of Bectileth. He went from Bectileth along the mountain on the northern side, above Cilicia.
He took his entire army—infantry, cavalry, and his chariots—and went from there toward their territories.
He killed the people of Put and Lud and took captive all the descendants of Rassis and the descendants of Ishmael who lived in the wilderness south of Eleon.
He crossed the Euphrates, passed through Mesopotamia, and plundered all their great cities above the cities of [?], until he reached the region.
He reached the territory of Cilicia and killed all his enemies. He went as far as the territory of Japheth, toward the southwest.
He hemmed in all the Midianites, plundered their livestock, and burned their houses.

He went down into the wilderness of Damascus at the time of the wheat harvest and burned all their fields. He ordered their sheep and pastures to be destroyed. He demolished their cities, took their children, and killed all their young men with the edge of the sword. Fear of him fell
and terror upon those who lived in Paralia, those in Sidon and Tyre, and all those who lived in Damanahon. Those in Azotus and Ashkelon were also greatly afraid of him.
They sent messengers with words of peace,
saying, “Here we are before you, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar the great king. Deal with us as you wish here in your presence.
Look, our cities, all our settlements, all our fields and pastures, and all the enclosures for our cattle and sheep are yours, before you. Do whatever you wish.
Look, our great cities and those who live in them are your servants. Come and do as you wish.”
Those men reached Holofernes and reported this message to him.
He and his army went down into their territories. He secured their great cities and took chosen men from among them to accompany them.
They and all their settlements welcomed him with garlands, singing, psalms, and drums.

He went around their territories and broke their images. He had been commanded to destroy all the people's gods, so that they would worship Nebuchadnezzar alone, and all nations and all territories would call him God.
He came into the whole plain of Esdraelon at Gabaya, opposite the great ridge of Judea.
He went through the wilderness of Tebon and the towns of Sekton. He stayed there for one month, gathering provisions for his troops.

The Israelites and those who lived in Judea heard everything that Holofernes, the commander of the army of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia, had done to the nations: how he had devastated all their territories and destroyed them.
They were exceedingly afraid of him, and they feared for Jerusalem and for the house of the Lord their God.

For all the chosen people of the tribe of Judah had only recently come up after being taken captive. They were also concerned for the sacred vessels, the altar, and the sanctuary, because they had consecrated it after it had been defiled.
He sent word throughout all the territory of Syria, Konas, Beth-horon, Belmon, Jericho, Askoban, Esora, and the valley of Salem.
He reached all the peaks of their high mountains and camped above the towns in them. They took provisions for war, since their harvest had just taken place.
And Joakim, the high priest who was in Jerusalem in those days, wrote to those living in Bethulia and Betomesthaim, which faces Jericho, toward the wilderness near Dothan.

He said, “Fortify the mountain passes, for through them lies the entrance into Judea, so that you may prevent them from passing through. Its entrances and paths are narrow, allowing only two men to pass abreast.”
And the Israelites did as Joakim the high priest and all the elders of Israel who lived in Jerusalem commanded them.
And all the Israelites cried out to the Lord with a loud voice and subjected themselves to great suffering.
They, their wives, their children, their livestock, every foreigner and resident alien, and everyone acquired by purchase [?] put on sackcloth.

And all the men of Israel, their wives, and their children who lived in Jerusalem fell down in the sanctuary, put dust on their heads, spread out their sackcloth before the Lord, and covered the altar with sackcloth.

Together they cried out earnestly to the Lord, the God of Israel, that their children might not be carried off as plunder, their wives taken captive, the cities of their inheritance destroyed, or their sanctuary defiled and made a spectacle for the nations.
And the Lord saw their suffering and heard their cry. The people fasted for many days throughout Judea and in Jerusalem before the sanctuary of the Lord, who rules over all.

Joakim the high priest, all the priests who stood before the Lord, and those who performed the Lord’s service tied sackcloth around their waists and offered the regular sacrifice, the offerings made in fulfillment of vows, and the freewill offerings that the people brought.
They put dust on their heads and cried out to the Lord with all their strength, saying, “Look with favor upon the house of Israel.”

And they reported to Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, saying, “The Israelites have prepared for war, closed the passes, fortified the high mountain peaks, and placed obstacles along the roads.”
He became extremely angry and summoned the leaders of Moab, the rulers of Ammon, and the leaders of the coastal region.

He said to them, “Tell me, people of Canaan, who are these people who live in the mountains? Who are those who live there, and how large is their army? What is their source of strength, and who is the king established over them, or their ruler, or their commander?”
“And why, of all those who live in the west, have they not come to welcome me?”

And Achior, the ruler of all the Ammonites, said to him, “My lord, hear a word from your servant’s mouth, and I will tell you the truth about this people who live in the mountains near you. No lie will come from your servant’s mouth.
“These people came from the Chaldeans.
“They formerly lived in Mesopotamia, because they did not wish to follow the gods of their ancestors who were in the land of the Chaldeans.

“They abandoned the way of their relatives and worshiped the God of heaven, the Lord whom they had come to know and who brought them out from the power of their gods. They fled to Mesopotamia and lived there for many days.

“Their God told them to leave the place where they had settled as foreigners and go to the land of Canaan. They went to the land of Canaan and lived there for many days, accumulating gold, silver, and very many livestock.

“They went down into the land of Egypt because famine had covered the land of Canaan. They stayed there while they were being fed, and they multiplied there and became so numerous that their people could not be counted.
“Then the king of Egypt rose against them, dealt craftily with them, afflicted them, forced them to labor at brickmaking, and made them slaves.
“They cried out to their God, and he struck the whole land of Egypt with an incurable plague and brought them out of Egypt, away from [?].
“And the Lord dried up the Red Sea before them.
“He led them into Sinai and Kadesh-barnea and drove out all those who lived in the wilderness.
“They settled in the land of the Amorites, and he destroyed all the people of Heshbon by his power. They crossed the Jordan and took possession of all their territory.
“He drove out before them the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Hittites, the people of Shechem, and all the Girgashites, and they lived there for many days.
As long as they did not sin before their God, all prosperity remained with them, because the Lord, who hates injustice, was with them.

But when they abandoned the way he had commanded them to follow, he destroyed them and scattered them through many wars, with overwhelming severity. They were taken captive to a foreign land, the house of their God was plundered and became a wasteland, and their enemies seized their cities.

But now they have returned to their God and have gathered there from the places where they were scattered. They have settled in Jerusalem, where their sanctuary is, and have also settled in the mountains, because the land was deserted.

And now, my lord, if these people have sinned and there is some offense they have committed against their God, let us investigate it together, for this will be their downfall. Then let us go up and fight them.
But if these people have committed no offense, do not attack them, my lord, lest the Lord strengthen them and their God stand up for them, and we become a disgrace throughout all the territories.

When Achior had finished saying these things, all the people standing around the tent began to grumble. Holofernes’ commanders and all those who lived in Paralia and Moab said that they should kill him.
They said, “We are certainly not afraid of the Israelites, a people who have neither the strength nor the power to fight against a mighty army.
Let us simply go up, and they will become food for your whole army, our lord Holofernes.”
Then, when the men around the assembly had fallen silent, Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, spoke to Achior before all the foreigners and all the people of Moab.
“Leader of Ephraim, how can you prophesy to us today and tell us, ‘Do not attack the Israelites, because the Lord will strengthen them’? Who is the Lord except Nebuchadnezzar?

He will send his messengers and destroy them and scatter them from the face of the earth, and their God will not save them. We, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, will crush them as though they were a single man, and they will not withstand the strength of our cavalry.

For with it we will trample them. Their mountains will be drunk with their blood, and their dead will be many. Their children will not stand on their feet before us, but they will be utterly destroyed from the earth. King Nebuchadnezzar, lord of the whole earth, has spoken, for he said that his word would not [?].

But you, Achior, leader of Ammon, who have spoken these words today, will not see my face from today—from this very day—because of your sin, until I take vengeance on those who came out of the land of Egypt.
At that time the iron weapons of my army and my people will pierce your side, and you will fall among their dead.
When I return, my servants will take you into their mountains and leave you in one of their cities on the heights.
They will not kill you until I crush them.
Since you are confident in your heart that we cannot overcome them, do not be downcast. For I have spoken, and not one of my words will fail.”
Holofernes commanded his servants who stood before him in his tent to take Achior, send him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites.
His servants took him and led him outside the tent into the wilderness. He went through the wilderness into the mountains, and then they reached the springs below Bethulia.
When the men of that city saw them from the mountaintop, they took their weapons and went out of the city to the mountaintop. All the slingers guarded the passes and hurled stones down at them.
They loosened Achior’s bonds and tied him at the foot of the mountain. They left him abandoned there below the mountain and returned to their lord.
The Israelites came down from their cities, went to him, untied him, and brought him to Bethulia. They placed him among the officials of their cities.
Those in office in those days were Uzziah son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon, and Chabris son of Gothoniel.

They summoned all the elders of their cities, and all their young men and their women hurried to their assembly. They stood Achior in the midst of them all, and Uzziah questioned him about everything that had happened.

He answered them and told them everything Holofernes had said, all that they had discussed, all the words spoken among the Assyrian officials, and how arrogantly Holofernes had spoken against the house of Israel.
All the people fell down and bowed before the Lord on their faces.
They cried out and said, “Lord, God of heaven, look at their insults, have mercy on the suffering of our people, and look with favor upon your sanctuary this day.”
They encouraged Achior and praised him greatly.
Uzziah took him from the assembly and brought him into his house. He made a feast for the leaders, and throughout that whole night they called upon the God of Israel to help them.
On the next day Holofernes commanded his entire army and all his people who fought alongside him to march to Bethulia, advance into the mountain passes, and fight against the Israelites.

At that time all their strong and mighty men came down: 170,000 fighting men on foot and 12,000 mounted men, not counting the baggage and the men who did not come down, a very large number of foot soldiers.
They camped in the valley beside Bethulia, near the spring. Their camp extended lengthwise as far as Dothan and Belmaim, and across from Bethulia as far as Cyamon, which faces Esdraelon.

When the Israelites saw how numerous they were, they were terrified and said to one another, “These men will now cover the whole face of the earth. Nothing can bear their weight—not the mountains, the hills, or the lowlands.”
They all took up their military equipment, lit fires in their fortifications, and kept watch throughout that night.
On the second day Holofernes brought out all his cavalry before the Israelites who were in Bethulia.
He sent scouts to examine the open spaces around their towns and inspect their springs, to reach those places before him and have fighting men camp there. He himself hurried there with his army.
All the leaders of the descendants of Esau, all the princes of the house of Moab, and the rulers of Paralia came to him.
They said to him, “Listen to our words, my lord, so that your army will not suffer destruction.
For these people, the Israelites, do not rely on their spears, but on their fortresses and the mountains where they live, because there is no way to climb their mountains.
And now, my lord, do not fight them in open battle, and none of your people will die—not a single man.
Instead, wait for them with your army. Let all the fighting men of your forces keep watch, and let your men secure all their springs that flow from the foot of the mountain.

For all the inhabitants of Bethulia draw water from there. Thirst will kill them, and they will fall back. We and our people will go up close to their fortresses and to the mountaintops. We will camp there and keep watch over them so that none of them—not a single man—can come out of their towns.
They, their wives, and their children will perish from hunger without anyone fighting them, and they will be scattered along the streets of their towns.
You will take harsh revenge on them because they rebelled and did not receive you peacefully.”
Their words pleased Holofernes and all his men, and he ordered them to do as they had proposed.
The Ammonites moved their camp, and with them were 5,000 Assyrians. They camped in the valley and seized control of the Israelites’ water supplies and springs.

The descendants of Esau and the Ammonites went up and camped in the mountains opposite Dothan. They sent some of their men toward the southwest and east, opposite Egrebel, which is beside Chusi, near the Mochmur brook. The rest of the Persian army camped in the plain and covered the whole face of the earth. Then they surrounded their camp and their equipment with a vast number of men, whom no one could outnumber.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord their God, because they were deeply distressed. All their enemies had surrounded them, and they had no way to escape from among them.

The Assyrians remained with their entire army, keeping them surrounded—their infantry, their chariot troops, and their cavalry—for three and four [?] days. All the water containers of the inhabitants of Bethulia were emptied.
They had no water to drink that would satisfy their thirst, and they began drinking measured rations.
Their children, their wives, and their young men grew weak and wasted away from thirst. They fell in the city squares and in the approaches to the gates, and they no longer had any strength.
All the people gathered against Uzziah and the leaders of the town—the young men, the women, and the children. They cried out loudly and spoke before all their elders.
May God judge between us and you, because you have done us a great wrong by not speaking of deliverance through peace with the Assyrians.
“Now the one who helps us has failed us. God has handed us over to them so that we fall before them from thirst, in utter ruin.
Now make terms with them and surrender all your towns. Let the army of Holofernes and all his forces plunder them.
For it is better for us to be plundered and become their slaves, so that we remain alive and do not see our children die before our own eyes. The lives of our wives and children are wasting away.

Look, we call heaven and earth and the God of our ancestors as witnesses against you—he who judges us according to our sins and the sins of our ancestors—not to do this thing today, on this very day.”
There was great weeping among their assembly. They all wept together and cried out loudly to the Lord.
Uzziah said to them, “Have confidence, our brothers, and be patient for five more days, until the Lord our God turns his mercy toward us, for he will not abandon us forever.
If those days pass and his help has not come to us, we will do as you say.”
He dispersed the people to their posts, their fortifications, and the quarters of their city. They went and sent their women and those who were very ill into the city.

In those days Judith heard about this. She was the daughter of Merari, son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Ozian, son of Hilkiah, son of Ananias, son of Gideon, son of Reuel, son of Haqito, son of Elijah, son of Eliab, son of Nathanael, son of Shelumiel, son of Salasadai, son of Israel.
Her husband, Manasseh, was of her tribe and her city. He died during the barley harvest.

He had spent the day in the fields with those binding the sheaves. The heat struck his head and made him ill, and he took to his bed and died in Bethulia, his city. They buried him with his ancestors in their field at Dothan and Balamon.
Judith lived as a widow in her house for three [?] and four days.
She made herself a shelter on the roof of her house, tied sackcloth around her waist, and wore her widow’s clothes.

She fasted throughout her widowhood, except on the day before the Sabbath and on the Sabbath, on the day before the new moon and on the new moon, and on the festivals and joyful celebrations of the house of Israel.
She was beautiful to look at, and her face was exceedingly lovely. Her husband Manasseh had left her gold and silver, male and female servants, livestock, and fields, and she managed them.
No one spoke an evil word against her, because she feared the Lord greatly.

She heard the evil things the people were saying against their ruler, because they had grown fainthearted when the water ran out. Judith also heard everything Uzziah had said to them, and how he had sworn to them that after five days they would surrender their city to the Persians.
She sent for and summoned her maid, who looked after all her possessions, and summoned Chabris and Charmis and the elders of her city.

They came to her, and she said to them, “Listen to me, rulers of the inhabitants of Bethulia. What you said before the people today was not right. By what you said, you established an oath between yourselves and God to surrender your city to your enemies if God did not help you within these five days.
Now who are you to put God to the test this very day and to stand between God and human beings?
Now God himself will question you, but you know nothing at all.

You do not know the depths of a human heart, and you cannot see the counsel of a person’s thoughts. How, then, can you search out God, who made all this? You want to know his heart and search out and discover his counsel! No, my brothers! Do not provoke the Lord our God.
Even if he chooses to help us within these five days, he has the power to save us however he wishes, whether throughout all our days or to destroy us before our enemies.
But you must not try to dictate to the Lord your God, because God is not like a human being who can be coerced, nor is he like a mortal who takes offense.
Instead, wait for salvation from him, and call upon him to help us and hear our voice, if he is willing to save us.
For no such thing has arisen in our days, nor is there today any people, tribe, region, or city among us that worships gods made by human hands, as happened in former days.
Because of that, our ancestors were given over to war and plunder, and they suffered a great defeat before their enemies.
But we have no other God besides him, and we trust in him not to disregard us or our kin.
For if he captures us, he will do the same to Judah, and all our holy places will be plundered. He will demand an account of their defilement from their own mouths.

Our brothers will be killed, our country taken captive, and our inheritance laid waste by whoever enters our inheritance. Among the nations where we are enslaved, we will be a stumbling block and a disgrace before those who acquire us.
Our captivity will bring no praise, for the Lord our God has seen our humiliation.
And now, our brothers, tell our fellow citizens, for they listen to us, and their lives depend on us. The sanctuary and the altar also rest upon us.”
And in all this, let us give thanks to God, who tests us as he tested our fathers.
Remember everything he did with Abraham, how greatly he tested Isaac, and what happened to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria while he was tending the sheep of Laban, his mother's brother.
For it was not when he tested those men that he examined their hearts [?]. Nor has he oppressed us; rather, God disciplines those who draw near to him in order to instruct them.
And Uzziah said to her, "Everything you have said, you have spoken with a good heart, and no one can oppose your words.
For your wisdom has not been heard only today. Rather, from your earliest days everyone has known your wisdom, because the disposition of your heart is blessed.
Nevertheless, the people were extremely thirsty and compelled us to do as they told us. They imposed on us an oath that we cannot break.
And now pray for us, because you are a woman who fears God, so that God may send rain and fill our cisterns, and we will no longer be thirsty."
And Judith said to them, "Listen to me, and I will do something that will be told from generation to generation.
Stand at the gate tonight, and I will go out with my maid. Within the days in which you said you would hand over the city to our enemy, the Lord, the God of Israel, will help us through my hand.
But do not ask me what I will do, for I will not tell you until I have finished what I am going to do."
And Uzziah and their officials said to her, "Go in peace. May God be with you and take vengeance on our enemy before you."
And they returned and went to their companions.

But Judith fell with her face to the ground, put dust on her head, and exposed the sackcloth she was wearing. She brought an offering into the house of God in Jerusalem for the regular incense offering at that time [?], and she cried out loudly at that time.

And Judith said, "Lord, God of my father, hear me, you who put a spear into Simeon's hand to take vengeance on the enemies who violated the womb, defiled virginity, plundered, and profaned the womb shamefully. It must not be like this, ever [?].
Yet they did it. For you gave their officers power for slaughter [?], and the bed was spread with the blood of those who were killed—the strong servants and mighty men, from their couches [?].

Their wives and daughters were taken captive, and their plunder was divided among the children who were loved by you, who burned with your zeal, recoiled from their polluted blood, and called on you to help them. Lord my God, hear me, a widow.

For you made what came before this, those things, and what came afterward. You knew what is happening now and what is to come, those things and what came afterward, what is happening now and what is to come; and it happened according to what you knew.
Your counsel is right, and they said to you, 'Look, you have come.' For all your ways are fitting, and you have pronounced your judgment according to what you knew.

For look, the Persians have become numerous with their forces. They have mounted their horses, and their riders have grown strong through their arms. Their foot soldiers have trusted in their armor, their spears, their bows, and their slings. They do not know that you are God, who crushes wars, and that the Lord is your name.

You scattered them and their forces by your power. Drown their strength in your wrath, for they planned to defile your sanctuary and profane the tabernacle, the resting place of your glorious name, and they tore off the horns of your altar with iron.
Look at their arrogance and send your wrath upon their heads. Give strength to my hand, to me, a widow.
Through what I have planned, I will kill the servant, the officer, and his young attendant with deceitful lips. Bring down their stature by a woman's hand.

For your strength does not depend on great numbers, nor your power on strong men. Bring them low, Lord, for you are the helper of the few, the helper of the weak, the savior of the destitute, and the one who gives life to the despairing.
Yes, Lord, God of my father and God of Israel's inheritance, Lord of heaven and earth, creator of the waters, you are king over all your works. Hear my prayer.
Make my words deceive, wound, and kill the enemies of your law, your holy temple, the summit of Zion, and the dwelling place of your children—those who have planned terrible things."
And cause all your people to know and recognize that you are God, the Lord of all, and that there is no other besides you who gives strength to the people of Israel.
And then, when she had finished crying out to the Lord, the God of Israel,
and had finished saying all these things, she rose from where she had fallen, called her maidservant, and went down into her house, where she stayed on Sabbaths and feast days.

She took off the sackcloth she wore and put on her widow's clothing. She washed her body with water, anointed herself with perfume, arranged the hair of her head, and adorned herself with her headdress. Then she put on the festive clothes she used to wear when her husband Manasseh was alive.
She put on her sandals and adorned herself with bracelets, rings, necklaces, and all her finery. She made herself very beautiful, enough to captivate the eyes of every man who saw her.
She gave her maidservant a wineskin and a jar of oil to carry. She filled a bag with flour, figs, and fine wheat bread, packed all her provisions, and had her carry them.
She went toward the entrance of Bethulia and found Uzziah and the elders of the city, Chabris and Charmis, standing there.
When they saw how remarkably her appearance had changed and how she was dressed, they were utterly astonished at her beauty.
They said to her, “May the God of Israel grant you favor to accomplish what you have planned for the strengthening of the children of Israel and Jerusalem.”

She said to them, “Give orders for the city gate to be opened for me, so that I may go out and carry out what I have spoken about with you.” And they ordered their companions to open it for her, as she had requested.
They did so, and Judith went out with her maid. The people of the city watched her until she had descended the mountain and passed through the valley, and they could no longer see her.
She went straight through the valley, and the Persian guards found her.

They seized her and questioned her, saying, “Who are you? Where are you going, and where have you come from?” She said to them, “I am a daughter of the Hebrews, and I have fled from them, since they intend to surrender their city to you.

I have come ahead to Holofernes, the commander of your army, to tell him the truth and show him the route by which you can go and take possession of all their territory without a single one of your men being wounded.”
When those men heard her words and looked at her face, her beauty was exceedingly wonderful in their eyes.
They said to her, “You have saved your life by hurrying down to our lord. Now go to his tent, and we will send some of us with you to bring you to him.
When you stand before him, do not be afraid. Tell him what you have told us, and he will treat you well.”
They chose a hundred men from among them and escorted her and her maidservant. They brought her to Holofernes so that they could inform him about her.

They marveled at her beauty and were astonished at the children of Israel because of her. They said to one another, “Who would despise these people when they have such women among them? It would not be good to leave even one of their men alive, for those left alive could outwit the whole earth.”
Those who were staying with Holofernes and all his attendants came out, and they brought her into his tent.
Holofernes was lying on his bed, with a coverlet adorned with fine gold cloth, emeralds, and very costly pearls.
They told him about her, and he came out [?], while golden lamps shone before him.

When Judith came to him, his attendants were standing there, and they were all astonished at the beauty of her face. She fell facedown on the ground and bowed before him, and his servants raised her up.
Holofernes said to her, “Take courage, woman, and do not let your heart be afraid, for I do not harm anyone who submits to serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole world.”
“Now, if these people of yours who live in the mountains had not rebelled against me, I would not have taken up arms against them. But they brought this on themselves.
Now tell me why you fled from them and came to us. You have indeed come to save your life. Be assured that from this night onward you will live.
And if there is anyone who would treat you harshly [?], we will do you nothing but good, we will do you nothing but good, as we do to the servants of our lord, King Nebuchadnezzar.”
Judith said to him, “Listen to the words of your maidservant, and let your maidservant speak before you. Your maidservant will not tell my lord a lie tonight.”
If you follow the words of your servant, God will bring the undertaking to completion, and nothing of what you have planned will fail, my lord.

As surely as Nebuchadnezzar lives, who rules over all the earth, and as surely as his power lives, which sent you to set everything in order, it is not only human beings who serve him through your greatness. The wild beasts, livestock, and birds of the sky also submit because of your power and sustain Nebuchadnezzar and his whole household.

For we have heard of your deeds, and it has been heard throughout the earth that you alone are excellent in all his kingdom, that you are mighty in all your deeds, and that you are astonishing in all your battles.
And now we have heard the words that Achior spoke to you in your camp. The people of Bethulia kept him alive, and he told them everything he had said to you.

And now, my lord, do not disregard his words, but take them to heart, for it is truly as he said. No one can take vengeance on this people, nor can warfare kill them, unless they sin against their God.
And now, so that my lord may not be misled or unsuccessful, their death will overtake them before you through this sin by which they have angered their God with their wrongdoing.
For their food and their supplies of water have run out, and they have begun to eat their livestock. They are determined to eat all these things that their God forbade them to eat in their law.

They have set their minds on the firstfruits of their grain and the tithes of their wine and oil, which they had kept and consecrated for the priests who stand in Jerusalem before our God. None of the people is permitted even to touch these with their hands.
They have sent to Jerusalem, because those who are there are also doing this, and have received permission from the leaders and rulers.
When they have told them and they have done this, on that very day he will deliver them into your hands.
When I learned all this, I, your servant, withdrew from them, and God sent me to do with you a deed that, when people hear of it, will make the whole earth tremble.

For I, your servant, fear the Lord and am devoted to the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, day and night. Give the command and say, ‘Do not hinder her.’ Now I will stay with you, my lord, but at night I, your servant, will go out into the wilderness to pray to the Lord, and he will tell me when they have committed their sin.
Then I will come and inform you, and you will march out with your whole army, and no one will oppose you.

I will lead you through the midst of Judea until you arrive before Jerusalem. You will establish your throne in its midst, gather them together, and take them like sheep whose shepherd has abandoned them. Not even a dog will lick with its tongue before you. For these things were told and made known to me, and, knowing them, I was sent to tell you.
Her words were pleasing to Holofernes and to all the people, and they marveled at her wisdom.
They said, “From one end of the earth to the other, there is no woman like this one in the beauty of her face and the wisdom of her words.”

Holofernes said to her, “God has done well for you by sending you ahead of your people, so that you may be under the protection of our hands, while those who rebelled against my lord face death and destruction.”

“And now, you are beautiful in appearance and blessed in your speech. If you do as you say, your God will be my God, and you will live in Nebuchadnezzar’s house, and your name will be exalted throughout the earth.”
He ordered them to bring her into the place where the silver vessels were kept, and ordered them to feed her from the food prepared for him and give her some of his wine to drink.
Judith said, “I will not eat any of it, lest it become a sin for me. Instead, I will eat what I have brought.”
Holofernes said to her, “But if what you have brought with you runs out, where shall we obtain more of the same to give you? None of your people is here with us.”
Judith said to him, “As you live, my lord, your servant will not use up what she has with her before God accomplishes through my hands what he has planned.”
Holofernes’ servants brought her into a tent, and she spent the night there and slept until midnight.
She rose at that hour, and after the night watch she sent word to Holofernes, saying, “My lord, give orders that they allow your servant to go out.”

Holofernes ordered those guarding her not to hinder her. After this she stayed in the camp for three days. At night she would go out into the valley of Bethulia and bathe at the spring of water in the camp.
When she came up, she would pray to the Lord, the God of Israel, to direct her way so that the people of her nation would not be taken captive.
Then she would return and remain purified in the camp, and each evening she would eat.
Then, on the fourth day, Holofernes gave a feast for his own servants alone. He invited no outsiders and no one else to the feast.
He said to Bagoas, his steward, the eunuch in charge of all his possessions, “Persuade this Hebrew woman who is with you to come to us and eat and drink with us. Go to her and speak to her.”
“For it would be a disgrace to us if, having found such a woman, we did not speak to her. If we do not win her, they will laugh at us.”

Bagoas left Holofernes and went to her and said, “Do not hesitate, my beautiful daughter, to come to my lord, to be honored in his presence, drink wine with him, and enjoy yourself. Today you will be to him like one of the Assyrian women who attend in Nebuchadnezzar’s house.”
Judith said to him, “Who am I, and what is my family, that I should oppose my lord? Everything that pleases you in your sight I will do promptly, and it will be a joy to me until the day I die.”

She rose, made herself beautiful, put on her clothes, and adorned herself with all a woman’s ornaments. Her maid went with her and spread her bedding on the ground before Holofernes. She had received it from Bagoas, who had spread it for her in her lodging so that she could recline on it when she ate.
Judith came in and reclined. Holofernes' heart was stirred by her, and he longed intensely to sleep with her. From the time he had seen her, he had been waiting for an opportunity.
Holofernes said to her, “Drink with us and enjoy yourself.”
Judith said to him, “I will drink, my lord, for today my life means more to me than on any day since I was born.”
She took what her maid had prepared for her and ate and drank in his presence.
Holofernes was delighted because of her and drank a great deal of wine, more than he had ever drunk on any single day since he came into existence and was born.

When evening came, his servants hurried to leave. Bagoas closed the tent from outside and dismissed those who attended his master. They went to their quarters, for they were all exhausted because they had drunk so much.
Judith was left alone with Holofernes in his tent. He was lying on his bed, for he had drunk excessively and was drunk.
Judith told her maid to go outside, stand by her quarters, and wait for her to come out at the usual time. “I will go out to pray,” she told her, and she told Bagoas the same thing.

Everyone left her, and no one, small or great, remained in his chamber. Judith rose, stood beside his bed, and said in her heart, “Lord, God of all power, look and act through my hands at this hour, so that Jerusalem may be exalted.”
“For the time has come for you to raise up your inheritance. Accomplish my plan for me, to overthrow the enemies who have risen against us.”
She went to Holofernes' bed, toward his head, and pulled away his pillow.
She stood over him, took hold of the hair of his head, and said, “My Lord, God of Israel, strengthen me today.”
She struck his neck again with all her strength and severed his head from him.
She pushed his corpse off the bed onto the ground, waited a little, and went out. She gave Holofernes' head to her maid.
She put it in her food bag, and the two went out together as they usually did for prayer. They passed beyond the enemy lookout in the valley, climbed the slope of Bethulia, and reached the city gate.
From a distance Judith said to those guarding the gate, “Open the gate! God is with us, to show his power again and give Israel strength against their enemies, as he has done today.”
When the people of the city heard her voice, they hurried down to the city gate and summoned the city's leaders.
They all ran, small and great, for they were astonished that she had returned. They opened the gate and welcomed her. They kindled a fire to give light and gathered around her.
She said to them in a loud voice, “Praise God, for he has not withdrawn his kindness and mercy from Israel, but has destroyed its enemy this night.”

She took his head out of her bag and showed it to them, saying, “Here is the head of Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, and here is the pillow on which he lay while drinking. God has killed him by the hand of a woman.”
“As the Lord lives, he guarded me on the journey I made to deceive him with my appearance so that he would die. He committed no sin against me and did not defile or disgrace me.”
All the people were greatly astonished. They bowed down and worshiped God, saying together, “Blessed are you, our God, today, on this day, for you have humiliated the enemies of your people.”

Uzziah said to her, “My daughter, you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth. Blessed is God, the Creator of heaven and earth, who helped you cut off the head of the commander of our enemies.”
“For your praise will never be erased from human hearts as they remember God's power forever.”

“May God make your name everlasting and watch over you with his goodness, because you did not spare your own life in the face of your people’s suffering, but went out to face death and walked uprightly before our God.” And the people said, “Amen and amen.”
Judith said to them, “Listen to me, my brothers. Take this head and hang it on the battlements of your fortifications.”

“Then, when morning dawns and the sun rises over the earth, all of you take your weapons of war. Let all the mighty men go outside the city, and appoint a commander for yourselves. And when you go down into the country toward the guards of the Assyrians—

“All of you take your weapons of war and carry them. When their guards see you, they will go to their camp to rouse the commanders of the Assyrian army and their forces. Then they will run to Holofernes’ tent and will not find him. Then they will be afraid and terrified and flee before you.
“But you and everyone living throughout the territory of Israel must pursue them and watch for them along all their roads.”
“Before you do this, summon Achior the Ammonite for me, so that he may see and recognize the man who defied the house of Israel and sent him to us to die with us.”
They summoned Achior from Uzziah's house. When he came and saw Holofernes' head in a woman's hand before the assembled people, he fell on his face, overcome with terror.

When they raised him up, he fell at Judith’s feet, bowed with his face to the ground, and said, “Blessed are you above all the great ones of Judah! All the peoples of the world will tremble when they hear your name.”
“Now tell us everything you have done during these days.” And Judith told them, in the midst of the people, everything she had done, from the day she went out until the day she returned.
When she finished her account, all the people shouted loudly and cried out joyfully in their towns.
When Achior saw everything God had done for Israel, he believed firmly in God, was circumcised, and joined the house of Israel, where he remains to this day.
When dawn broke and morning came, they hung Holofernes’ head on the battlements. They all took their weapons of war in their hands, went out, and confronted them toward the mountain ascent.
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent word to their commanders.
Their messengers, officials, and commanders went to Holofernes’ tent and said to his steward, “Wake our master, for the slaves have gone mad and have come down against us to fight us.”
Bagoas went in and knocked at the enclosure in front of the tent, for he thought that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith.
When no one answered him, he [?] and went into the chamber. He found his body lying on the ground, with his head no longer on it.
He cried out loudly, weeping and shouting. He wailed [?] and tore his clothes.
He went into the tent where Judith was staying and did not find her. He ran to his people, cried out to them, and said to them:

“The slaves have rebelled against us and [?] us! A single Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes’ corpse lies on the ground, and his head is no longer on him!”
When the commanders of the Assyrian army heard this news, they tore their clothes and were utterly terrified. They cried out and wailed very loudly in the midst of the camp.
When those who were in the camp heard, they too were terrified because of what had happened.
Fear and trembling seized them, and no one remained standing beside his companion. Instead, they all fled together in terror along every road, into the fields, and into the mountains.
Those in the camp and those in the mountains around Bethulia also heard and fled. Then all the Israelite fighting men rose and pursued them.

Uzziah sent messengers to Shiloh, Bethomasthaim, Bebai, Chobai, Chola, and throughout all the territory of Israel, to report what had happened and to urge everyone to come to their aid, pursue their enemies, and kill them.

When the Israelites heard, they all pursued them together and killed them as far as Choba. Those from Jerusalem and all their surrounding territories also came, because they had been told what had happened in their enemies’ camp. Those from Galilee and Gilead also pursued them and inflicted a great slaughter on them, until they had gone beyond Damascus and its territory.
The inhabitants of Bethulia went down into the Assyrian camps, plundered them, and became very wealthy.

Then the Israelites returned from the slaughter and plundered all the remaining estates, as well as their towns in the mountains and on the plain, for they had taken a large part of their territory from them for a long time.
Joakim the high priest came and brought up the Israelites who lived in Jerusalem. They came to see the good that the Lord had done for Israel, to see Judith, and to greet her.
When they came to her, they all blessed her together and said, “You are above Jerusalem! You are the greatness of the Israelites, and you are the pride of our people!
“For all this was accomplished by your hand, and I have done this good thing in Israel, and the Lord was pleased with them. May you be blessed forever and ever by the Lord, who rules over all.”

The people plundered their camps for three days. They gave Judith Holofernes’ tent and all the silver vessels. She took everything that was in it, loaded her mules and her chariots, and brought it in with her.
All the women of Israel ran to see her and bless her, and they held a great celebration for her. She took branches in her hand and gave them to the women who were with her, and they crowned her.
She went before all the people as the women sang, leading all the women. All the Israelites followed her with their weapons of war, crowning her and praising her with their mouths.
Judith spoke this song of praise before all Israel, and all the people responded with this praise.
Judith said, “Praise the Lord our God with the drum, and sing with cymbals. Make music to him with a psalm, exalt him with praise, and call upon his name.
“For the Lord crushes warfare, and the Lord is his name.
“His camp is among the people, and he has saved us from those who pursued us.
The Assyrians came from the mountains to the north. Their forces came out by the thousands; their numbers blocked the rivers, and their horses’ hooves covered the rocky ground.
“They said they would burn our territory with fire, kill our young men with the spear, take our children captive, and carry off our young women as plunder.”
And the Lord, who rules over all, killed them by the hand of a woman.

For their mighty warrior did not fall by the hand of a young man, nor did the sons of the Titans kill them, nor did great giants defeat them. Instead, Judith, the daughter of Merari, weakened him with the beauty of her face.
She left her widow’s clothes upon those who were mourning in Israel.
She anointed her face with perfume, braided her hair, and [?]. She put on festive clothes to deceive him and put on her sandals.
Her beauty captivated his eyes, and her cheeks took his soul captive. The sword passed through his neck.
The Persians were startled by her daring, and the Medes were afraid of her courage.
Then my afflicted ones cried out, and my sick ones were afraid and terrified and raised their voices.
The sons of my daughters pursued them and struck them. Their young men also hurled stones at them, and they perished in the Lord’s battle.
I will proclaim praise to the Lord; I will proclaim new praise to the Lord.
The Lord is great and exceedingly glorious, and his power is astonishing.
Let all your works praise you, for you spoke and they came into being. You sent your spirit and they were formed, and there is nothing that does not obey your word.
For the foundations of the mountains shake, and the heavens also shake. The rocks melt like wild honey before your face, yet you show favor to those who fear you.
For no sacrifice is sufficient for a pleasing fragrance, and all the fat is too little for your offering. But whoever fears the Lord is great at all times.
Woe to the nations that rise against my people! The Lord, who rules over all, will take vengeance on them on the day of judgment.
He will send fire and worms into their flesh, and they will weep in pain forever.
When they reached Jerusalem, they worshiped God. After they had purified themselves, the people brought their offerings and their voluntary gifts.
Judith deposited all the possessions of Holofernes that the people had given her.
The people rejoiced in Jerusalem before the sanctuary for three months, and Judith stayed with them.
After those days, everyone returned to his own property. Judith also returned to Bethulia and lived on her estate, and throughout her life she was honored in all the land.
Many desired her, but no man had sexual relations with her throughout her life after her husband Manasseh died and was buried among his people.
She grew very old.
She grew old in the house of her husband Manasseh, reaching one hundred and [?].
The house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before she died, she divided her possessions among all the relatives of her husband Manasseh and her own close relatives.
No one frightened the Israelites during Judith’s lifetime, nor for many days after she died.
